body: 内閣府が16日発表した2026年7～9月期の国内総生産（GDP、季節調整済み）の速報値は、物価の変動を除いた実質で前期比0・02％減となり、この状態が1年続いた場合の年率換算は0・1％減だった。【図解でわかる】インフレとデフレ　そもそもどういうこと？マイナス成長は4四半期ぶり。デジタル需要などを背景にした企業の設備投資は堅調だったものの、大雨などの天候不順や長引く物価高などで個人消費が低迷した。事前の市場の予測（13機関平均で前期比0・0％増）を下回った。GDPの過半を占める個人消費は前期比0・3％減で、2四半期連続のマイナスとなった。設備投資は1・6％増、輸出は0・2％減だった。【大原翔】

title: 福岡市長選 再選挙が確実に
body: きのう行われた福岡市長選挙は、有効投票数の4分の1を超える候補者がなく、再選挙となることが確実となりました。【写真で見る】各候補者の得票数　福岡市長選13人という過去最多の立候補者となった福岡市長選挙は、投票率が45.58%と、前回4年前の34.31%を11.27ポイント上回りました。開票の結果、元衆議院議員の稲富修二氏が、13万7667票とトップの得票となりました。公職選挙法では、有効投票数の4分の1を超える得票を得た候補者がいない場合は再選挙が行われることになっています。最多得票の稲富氏の得票は、有効投票数59万2723票の4分の1を超えませんでした。福岡市選挙管理委員会はきょう選挙会を開催して選挙結果を確定しますが、福岡市長選挙は再選挙になることが確実となりました。

title: フアン氏がNVIDIA復帰協議 報道
body: [１５日 ロイター] - 英紙フィナンシャル・タイムズ（ＦＴ）は１５日、米半導体大手エヌビディ‌アの最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）を辞任したジ⁠ェンスン・フアン氏が復帰を検討しており、側近らとその可能性について協​議したと報じた。事情に詳しい関係者の話として伝えた。フアン氏の側‌近の１人はＦＴに対し、同氏の復帰を働きかけるため、シリコンバレーの経営幹部ら‌による「作戦本部」を‌立ち上げており、ホワイト​ハウスの支持も取り付けたいと語った。この側近は「‌最先端の研究所を除けば、テクノロジー業界の有力者は皆、‌ジェンスンが大​好きだ」と述べ、こうした取り組み‌はフアン氏の支持を得ていると説明した。ＦＴは１３日、エヌビデ⁠ィアの取締役会がフアン氏の後任探しの一環で、英半導体設計大手アーム・ホールディングスのレ⁠ネ・ハースＣＥＯに接触したと報じ​ていた。エヌビデ‌ィアは通常の営業時間外で、コメント要請に直ちに応じなかった。フアン氏は複数の不倫関係⁠が発覚したことを受け、１２日に辞任した。この⁠うち１件は中国のスパイと疑われる人物との関係で、⁠同社の先端人工知能（ＡＩ）半導体の対中輸出を巡る疑問‌が浮⁠上した。これを受けて同社は危機に陥り、​フアン氏が資金面で支えてきたＡＩ業界にも衝撃が広がった。

title: JSR売却 差益9000億円超の見込み
body:
官民ファンド・産業革新投資機構（ＪＩＣ）が、傘下に置く半導体材料大手ＪＳＲを三井化学に売却する案件で、株式売却による差益が９０００億円超と見込まれることがわかった。政府関係者によると、政府保有株の配当などを財源に民間事業に出資する「産業投資」としては、過去最大級の利益となる。【画像】三井化学、半導体材料大手ＪＳＲの買収発表
買収は９日に発表されたが、ＪＩＣは各案件の詳細な収益を開示していない。関係者によると、ＪＩＣは約５５００億円を投資。三井化学が公表した株式価値（１兆３９２１億円）に、手続き終了時までにＪＳＲが生む経済的価値などが加わり、ＪＩＣが回収できる額は少なくとも１・４兆円を上回る見通しだ。
ＪＳＲは、半導体基板に回路を作る際に欠かせないフォトレジスト（感光剤）の世界市場でトップクラスのシェア（占有率）を持つ。半導体は高市内閣が掲げる戦略１７分野の一つで、政府関係者は「官民ファンドが仲立ちし、半導体素材企業の統合が進む第一歩となった」と評価している。

title: コンテナホテル8年で145店舗 背景
body:
国道沿いやインターチェンジの近くで、コンテナホテルを次々と展開している企業がある。「HOTEL R9 The Yard」を運営するデベロップ（千葉県市川市）だ。11月10日には、茨城県筑西市に新店が開業。2018年に栃木県真岡市で1号店を開いてから、8年で145店舗に広がった。【画像】「コンテナホテルの客室」じっくり見るデベロップはもともと、建築用コンテナの製造を手掛けてきた。同社のホテル事業の売上高は2025年に86億円に達し、2026年は前年を上回るペースだという。駅から離れたホテルに、どんな人が泊まるのか。出店を続けられる理由はどこにあるのか。
広さ13平方メートルのコンテナが、そのまま1室になる。客室は1棟ずつ独立していて、隣の部屋と壁を共有しない。室内にはベッドやユニットバス、冷凍冷蔵庫、電子レンジなどを備え、部屋の前に車を止められる。料金は1泊6200円～だ。使うのは海上輸送用のコンテナではなく、梁と柱で組んだ建築用のコンテナだ。建物として登記できる構造で、耐震性も備える。同社によると、窓などを設けても必要な強度を確保できるという。平日は利用者の約9割をビジネス客が占める。「駅から遠い国道沿いやインターの近くに出店しているので、車で移動するビジネス客を想定している」と同社広報担当の麻生川佳奈さんは説明する。
出店先として狙うのは、工業団地や工場が集まるエリアだ。工場などでの作業に訪れた人が連泊するケースが多く、滞在は3日から1週間ほどが中心だ。同社によると開業から1年以上たった店舗の客室稼働率は、約8割に上る。参考までに、観光庁の『宿泊旅行統計調査』によると、2025年のビジネスホテルの客室稼働率は全国平均で75.3％だった。平日のビジネス利用が高い稼働率を支えているが、週末は誰が泊まっているのか。
客室はダブルとツインの2タイプがあり、40室の店舗なら、ダブル35室・ツイン5室ほどの配分だ。週末には家族連れや観光客に加え、ゴルフの前後に泊まる人も訪れる。客室数の少ないツインは、ダブルより先に埋まりやすいという。ツインはシングルベッド2台をL字型に置いた部屋で、未就学児はベッド1台につき1人まで添い寝できる。大人2人と未就学児2人の4人家族でも1室に泊まれる。「客室が1棟ずつ独立しているので、子どもが騒いでも周りを気にせずに済む。そこも選ばれる理由になっている」（麻生川さん）ツーリングの拠点にするライダーも多い。客室の前にバイクを止め、愛車とコンテナを一緒に撮影する人もいるという。そのほか、帰省の際に泊まる人や、飲み会で終電を逃した人の利用もある。

title: 米中露が会談へ 日本は蚊帳の外か
body:
深圳で18〜19日に開かれるAPEC首脳会議に合わせ、19日に史上初の米中露3カ国首脳会談が行われる。大国が世界外交を牛耳る「新ヤルタ会談」になるのではないか、日本は蚊帳の外に置かれ、3カ国の決めたことに従うしかなくなるのではないか、との見方も出ている。本当にそうなるのか。ホスト国・中国の視点から考える。
何らかの合意に至るとは想定していない。核兵器の削減に向けた入り口だ出典：読売新聞オンライン　2026/11/14(土)
中国はその交渉の枠組みに実質的に関与していないため、今回の会談でウクライナ問題を協議するのは適切ではないと思われる出典：ＡＦＰ＝時事　2026/11/14(土)
事前に用意された台本を首脳が読み上げる形式的な会談を要求している出典：読売新聞オンライン　2026/11/11(水)
「外国指導者と二国間会談を行う」としているが、具体的な予定については明らかにしていない出典：産経新聞　2026/11/13(金)
中国にとって、米国と並ぶ大国として扱われる舞台は歓迎だ。関係の深いロシアを同じ席に引き込めば発言力も増し、自尊心も満たされる。ホワイトハウスの発表後も中国当局は会談を確認していないが、集合写真と首脳声明には応じる構えと報じられている。
悩ましいのは、大国として何を話し、何を管理するかだ。米国が掲げる核兵器削減では、中国の核弾頭は約620発で米国の約6分の1にとどまり、2月には三者交渉を「不公平、不合理、実行不可能」と退けた。外交部は今週も、核軍縮を議題にするかとの質問をかわした。9月の米中首脳会談で対話開始が決まったAIのリスク管理も、追う側の中国は、いま競争を縛る約束には乗りにくい。ウクライナは議題から外れた。
大国の地位には強い関心を示しながら、大国としての具体的な責務は担いたくない、担えないのが今の中国だ。3カ国で決められることが乏しい以上、日本の頭越しの取引は起きにくい。むしろ日本はこの矛盾を突き、米中では決めきれない核やAIのルールを日本も加わる多国間の枠組みで作るよう、米国を含む各国を説得していく局面にある。

title: 米の「中国脅威論」どう生まれた
body:
米国のトランプ大統領は１９日、中国・深センで、習近平（シージンピン）国家主席と今年３回目の首脳会談に臨む。米国は、経済、軍事両面で大国化する中国への警戒を緩めていない。米国の対中脅威認識はどのように生まれたのか。
１９７２年２月、米国のリチャード・ニクソン大統領が訪中し、中国共産党主席の毛沢東と歴史的会談を行って米中関係を正常化させて以降、米国の対中外交は長らく「関与政策」を基調としてきた。
中国と経済・外交的な関係を深め、国際社会の秩序に引き入れれば、国内改革が進み、国際規範を尊重する国になると期待したためだ。米国の後押しで中国が２００１年１２月に世界貿易機関（ＷＴＯ）に加盟したのが象徴的だった。
貿易障壁が減ったことで外国企業の進出が進み、中国は「世界の工場」となった。中国は１０年、日本を抜いて名目国内総生産（ＧＤＰ）で世界第２位につけた。中国はこの時期、安全保障でも米国や周辺国を脅かし始めた。南シナ海の領有権主張を強め、東シナ海では日本に威圧的な態度をとるなど大国化への野望を隠さなくなった。
警戒を強めたオバマ政権は１１年１０月、中東からアジアに軸足を移すリバランス（再均衡）政策を発表した。当時のヒラリー・クリントン国務長官が米外交誌「フォーリン・ポリシー」で「政治の未来はアフガニスタンやイラクではなくアジアで決定される」とする論文を発表したのがそれだ。
米国の対中政策が抜本的に転換したのは、共和党のドナルド・トランプ氏が大統領に就任した１７年以降だ。
中国からの輸入増大により、米国の製造業が空洞化した。地方の製造業を中心に推計２４０万人の米国人が職を失った。トランプ氏は労働者の不満に目を向け、１５年６月１６日、米大統領選の共和党指名争いへの出馬を表明した記者会見で「中国は我々を滅ぼしている。中国から雇用を取り戻す」と述べた。大統領就任後は、中国に貿易戦争をしかけ、関税などで激しく対立した。

title: エストニア ロシアとの国境閉鎖へ
body: ［１５日　ロイター］ - エストニアのツアフクナ外相は１５日、隣国ロシアとの全ての‌国境検問所を１２月１日から閉鎖すると表明した。⁠エストニア政府は、自国の防衛関連企業に対する破壊工作未遂事​件にロシアが関与していると判断した。エストニア当局はこれに先‌立ち、ドローン（無人機）製造会社スリード・システムズに対する放火‌未遂の疑いで８人を拘‌束した。ロシア軍参謀本部​情報総局（ＧＲＵ）の指示によるものとしている。ツ‌ァフクナ氏はＸへの投稿で「ロシアはエストニアに対する‌敵対的行動には代​償が伴うことを理解しなければ‌ならない」と述べた。国境閉鎖がどのくらい⁠の期間続くのか、あるいは終了期日が設定されているかは言及しなかった。ロシア政府は、⁠欧州各国が指摘する妨害​工作への関与‌疑惑を一貫して否定している。ロシア外務省のザハロワ報道官は、国営通信タスに対⁠し、エストニアが実際に国境を閉鎖⁠すれば、「攻撃的で抑えの利かないロシア嫌⁠悪が一段と激化したことを示す」と述べた。エストニ‌ア公⁠共放送（ＥＲＲ）によると、エストニアには​現在、３カ所の国境検問所があり、歩行者や貨物の往来が可能。

title: 仏のデモおさまらず みえぬ打開策
body: フランスのマクロン政権が、全土で続くデモを鎮静化できないでいる。AFP通信によると、14日のデモには10万6千人が参加したと当局が発表。主催者側は20万人だったとしている。前週の当局発表の14万6千人から減少傾向にはあるものの、政権は有効な打開策を示せておらず、不満の解消は遠そうだ。【写真】二つのデモが映し出す、フランスのマクロン大統領の10年を読み解く9月に教育への投資を求めた高校生が始めた抗議は、生活費の高騰や政権への不満を訴えるデモへと拡大した。ロイター通信によると、政権は今月、最低賃金を月額1502ユーロ（約26万4千円）へ引き上げる方針を提示。だが、24ユーロ（4200円）の増額にとどまったため、100～150ユーロ規模の増額を求めた労組は反発。17日に再び抗議行動に出る構えを示した。警察による暴力も反発を招いている。AFPによると、9月以降、デモで警察官が使った催涙弾が14歳の少年の顔面に直撃するなど、10代を含む20人以上が重傷を負った。国会では、警察官らが武器を使う際に正当防衛だとみなしやすくする法案を審議中で、「殺害の許可だ」などと批判されている。14日のデモに参加したアドリアンさん（20）はAFPに、「抗議活動に参加するのが怖い。警察官の免責がさらに強まれば、私たちはもっと恐怖を感じるようになる」と語った。（疋田多揚）

title: 「中国の元スパイ」語る 接近手口
body:
アメリカの半導体大手エヌビディアのCEOを辞任したフアン氏と、不倫関係にあった中国のスパイとされる女性。いったい何者なのか。スパイの実態を追いました。
AI向けの半導体で世界をけん引するエヌビディア。ジェンスン・フアン氏（エヌビディアCEO当時）「いま私たちは新たな時代の始まりにいます。AI革命です」フアン氏は、創業から33年間、そのトップを務めたカリスマ経営者。トランプ大統領と親密な関係で、米中首脳会談にも同行した。しかし、12日、突然の辞任発表。世界に衝撃が走った。理由とされているのが、相次ぐ不倫問題の発覚だ。その相手の1人とされているのが、ピンクのワンピースの人物。アリス・フアン氏だ。ニューヨーク・タイムズは、アメリカの情報機関が中国のスパイと判断したと報じている。アリス氏はシンガポールのデータセンター企業の幹部で、エヌビディアの半導体を中国に不正に供給したとして捜査が進められている。アリス氏について中国政府は「アメリカがスパイ説をねつ造している」と主張している。一体、何者なのか。
13日、『news LOG』は台湾へ。エヌビディアの前CEO・ジェンスン・フアン氏と、アリス・フアン氏の2人が訪れていた場所を追跡取材した。台湾は、エヌビディアの前CEO・フアン氏が生まれ育った場所だ。よく買い物に訪れていたという商店街を訪ねると。LOG「あそこ見てください。フアンさんの写真がある」「めちゃくちゃニコニコしてる。お菓子、買ってる」飾られていたのは、フアン氏の写真やサイン。地元では英雄のような扱いだ。
これは去年、台湾で撮影されたアリス氏の映像。フアン氏に寄り添い笑みを浮かべている。この映像はどこで撮影されたのか。LOG「フアンさんはいるんですけど、あの写真の方がいないですね。」店側「アリスさんは見たことがありません」
そして...。見つけたのは完全予約制のレストラン。撮影された動画と同じ店だ。交渉すると、撮影が許可された。LOG「中を見ると、すごい高級っぽい店ですね」そこには、訪れたときに書いたというサインが。当時の様子について店の関係者は「フアン氏がアリス氏を厨房に連れてきた」と話したが、特に不審に思うことはなかったという。

title: 7-9月期実質GDP 4期ぶりマイナス
body: 内閣府が16日発表した2026年7～9月期の国内総生産（GDP、季節調整済み）の速報値は、物価の変動を除いた実質で前期比0・02％減となり、この状態が1年続いた場合の年率換算は0・1％減だった。【図解でわかる】インフレとデフレ　そもそもどういうこと？マイナス成長は4四半期ぶり。デジタル需要などを背景にした企業の設備投資は堅調だったものの、大雨などの天候不順や長引く物価高などで個人消費が低迷した。事前の市場の予測（13機関平均で前期比0・0％増）を下回った。GDPの過半を占める個人消費は前期比0・3％減で、2四半期連続のマイナスとなった。設備投資は1・6％増、輸出は0・2％減だった。【大原翔】

title: フアン氏がNVIDIA復帰協議 報道
body: [１５日 ロイター] - 英紙フィナンシャル・タイムズ（ＦＴ）は１５日、米半導体大手エヌビディ‌アの最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）を辞任したジ⁠ェンスン・フアン氏が復帰を検討しており、側近らとその可能性について協​議したと報じた。事情に詳しい関係者の話として伝えた。フアン氏の側‌近の１人はＦＴに対し、同氏の復帰を働きかけるため、シリコンバレーの経営幹部ら‌による「作戦本部」を‌立ち上げており、ホワイト​ハウスの支持も取り付けたいと語った。この側近は「‌最先端の研究所を除けば、テクノロジー業界の有力者は皆、‌ジェンスンが大​好きだ」と述べ、こうした取り組み‌はフアン氏の支持を得ていると説明した。ＦＴは１３日、エヌビデ⁠ィアの取締役会がフアン氏の後任探しの一環で、英半導体設計大手アーム・ホールディングスのレ⁠ネ・ハースＣＥＯに接触したと報じ​ていた。エヌビデ‌ィアは通常の営業時間外で、コメント要請に直ちに応じなかった。フアン氏は複数の不倫関係⁠が発覚したことを受け、１２日に辞任した。この⁠うち１件は中国のスパイと疑われる人物との関係で、⁠同社の先端人工知能（ＡＩ）半導体の対中輸出を巡る疑問‌が浮⁠上した。これを受けて同社は危機に陥り、​フアン氏が資金面で支えてきたＡＩ業界にも衝撃が広がった。

title: JSR売却 差益9000億円超の見込み
body:
官民ファンド・産業革新投資機構（ＪＩＣ）が、傘下に置く半導体材料大手ＪＳＲを三井化学に売却する案件で、株式売却による差益が９０００億円超と見込まれることがわかった。政府関係者によると、政府保有株の配当などを財源に民間事業に出資する「産業投資」としては、過去最大級の利益となる。【画像】三井化学、半導体材料大手ＪＳＲの買収発表
買収は９日に発表されたが、ＪＩＣは各案件の詳細な収益を開示していない。関係者によると、ＪＩＣは約５５００億円を投資。三井化学が公表した株式価値（１兆３９２１億円）に、手続き終了時までにＪＳＲが生む経済的価値などが加わり、ＪＩＣが回収できる額は少なくとも１・４兆円を上回る見通しだ。
ＪＳＲは、半導体基板に回路を作る際に欠かせないフォトレジスト（感光剤）の世界市場でトップクラスのシェア（占有率）を持つ。半導体は高市内閣が掲げる戦略１７分野の一つで、政府関係者は「官民ファンドが仲立ちし、半導体素材企業の統合が進む第一歩となった」と評価している。

title: そごう・西武大規模改装に400億円
body:
米投資ファンド傘下で経営再建を進める百貨店大手「そごう・西武」の劉勁（りゅうじん）社長が、読売新聞のインタビューに応じた。そごう４店舗と西武２店舗に計３００億～４００億円を投じ、２０２８年９月までに大規模改装を行う考えを示した。地方でもショッピングモールなどに小型百貨店の出店を加速するとし、反転攻勢に出る構えを強調した。【写真】高島屋とそごう・西武「明暗を分けた理由」
そごう・西武は２３年９月、セブン＆アイ・ホールディングスから、米投資ファンド「フォートレス・インベストメント・グループ」に売却された。劉氏はフォートレス出身で、今年４月に社長に就いた。
劉氏は「過去には数千億円の借金があって店舗などに投資ができなかった。構造改革でバランスシートが健全化し、稼いだキャッシュで店舗や人材、ＩＴに投資できるようになった」と述べた。
大規模改装中の西武池袋本店を除いた営業利益は、フォートレス傘下入り直前の決算期に５２億円の赤字だったが、２６年９月期には３９億円の黒字に転換しており、「各店舗が利益を生める体質になってきた」と手応えを語った。
大規模改装に着手するのは、横浜、千葉、広島、大宮のそごう４店舗と、東戸塚、福井の西武２店舗。千葉、大宮店などは約２０年ぶりで、福井店は１９７０年の開店以来初となる。残る所沢と秋田の西武２店舗も小規模な改装を行う。屋上庭園の整備やカフェの増設など、買い物以外でも楽しめる空間づくりを重視し、集客力の向上につなげる。
そごう横浜店については、改装後、「そごう横浜本店」に名称を変え、西武池袋本店とともに２本店体制とする。劉氏は「（池袋本店に頼る）一本足打法から脱却しないといけない。横浜店のポテンシャル（潜在能力）は高い」とし、２０３０年にも売上高を現状の１・５倍に伸ばす目標を掲げた。
今年９月に西武渋谷店を閉店したばかりの店舗網について、既存９店舗を縮小する考えは「（現時点で）ない」と述べた。

title: 大学発ベンチャー過去10年で3.5倍
body: 大学の研究成果を事業化する「大学発ベンチャー」が広がっている。経済産業省によると、令和7年度の企業数は6220社と、10年前の平成27年度から約3.5倍に増加した。少子化で学生獲得競争が激しくなる中、大学は収益源の確保や魅力向上を目指し、起業支援に力を入れる。【ひと目でわかる】就職氷河期世代はどのくらい冷遇されているのか昨年度のデータをみると、業種別では「IT（アプリケーション、ソフトウエア）」が1985社で最多。大学別では東京大が595社で首位となり、上位10校は首都圏や関西圏に集中する。地方大の伸びも目立ち、前年度比で岩手大は8.5倍、金沢大は4.9倍、開志専門職大（新潟市）は3.3倍となった。背景には大学経営の厳しさがある。文部科学省によると、18歳人口は平成4年の206万人をピークに減少し、大学進学者数も令和7年度の64.5万人から22年度には45.5万人に減ると推計される。8年度に定員割れした私立大は、集計した595校のうち46.2％の275校。国公立大も平成16年の法人化以降、交付金に頼りすぎない経営が求められている。大学発ベンチャーの先駆例として知られるのが、近畿大（大阪府東大阪市）の完全養殖クロマグロ「近大マグロ」だ。宮崎大発の「Smolt（スモルト）」は、規格外イチゴを餌の一部に活用して育てたサクラマスをブランド化した。研究成果を、大学の強みとして発信する動きも広がる。文科省の担当者は「生き残りをかけベンチャーに活路を見いだそうとする大学もある」と指摘。「研究成果を事業化し、社会にロールモデルとして示すことには大きな意義がある」と評価する。（藤崎真生）

title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
summary: The Ukrainian president says the slowed-down internet is making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.
body:
Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade Starlink service owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
body:
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the  company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.
"That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told  the Face The Nation programme.
Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
summary: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
body:
Mexican prison police secured the hospital where Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo was admitted earlier this week
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.
Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.
He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.
How one DEA killing began a brutal war
In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His death sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was placed under house arrest since 2022 and died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.

title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
summary: Han Won-seok, 34, confessed to using a hidden camera and AI to get a near-perfect mark on the significant test.
body:
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube channel of his lawyer
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."
When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.
Can smart glasses exam cheating be stopped?
A series of cases involving exam cheating with AI glasses in South Korea has universities and schools scrambling to rein in the use of the technology.
Han said he had only cheated to try and earn money and get a job that would make his parents proud of him again.
Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency told Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday that it was looking into the case.
"We received a written confession through the test taker's lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam," it confirmed in a statement.
It added that the case had now been assigned to investigators.
Because of the significance of the national exams, instances of cheating are not uncommon in South Korea, and cases involving the use of AI have become more prominent as the technology becomes more sophisticated.
Last month, two college applicants were reported to have used AI glasses to try and cheat their entrance exams at two Seoul universities.
Education ministry data also says there were four cases of cheating through AI glasses at middle and high schools in the past 12 months.

title: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
summary: The Pope took to the skies before arriving in Cusco on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour.
body:
Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.
Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".
On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.
There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."

title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
summary: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
body:
The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker.
Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers.
The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.
Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements.
"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.
The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.
The reset means they will be dismantled.
In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them".
Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power.
Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer
The prime minister has saidhe believes there is a "win-win" dealto be had with the EU.
Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food.
"This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said.
He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all.
Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork.
Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.
"The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said.
"If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union."
The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.
Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional £5bn.
The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.
This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading.
Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU
Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.
Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.
But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.
He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.
UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.
Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.
Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.
He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal".
Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.
"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.
Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.
Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.
"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.
"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

title: Cut national insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
summary: The report being launched this week will suggest gradually reducing employment costs over five years.
body:
Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill
National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say.
A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality.
Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise.
But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".
The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill.
Milburn has said the government spends £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.
He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales.
Milburn wants the government to providea legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support. Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits.
Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them.
The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.
But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow".
Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.
Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.
But Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and the minimum wage.
She said she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff.
Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".
Salon-owner Collette Osborne says she is "inundated" with CVs from young people
She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.
"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.
Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.
"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."
Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme he agreed with a recent move by Chancellor John Healey to slow down the equalisation of the national minimum wage across age groups.
Labour had pledged in its manifesto to remove "discriminatory age bands" and close the gap between adult minimum wages and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.
But in his Budget, Healey said pay for that age group would rise from £10.85 to £11.27 an hour in April next year while people aged 21 and over will see their wages increase from £12.71 to £13.21.
"I understand why because nobody wants to see young workers on poverty pay," Milburn said, but he said it "imposed a lot of costs on [the] government".
"I think we have got to look very carefully at the convergence issue," he said.
Milburn said he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.
"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.
"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."
On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.
People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.
McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".
But Whately said it is "just absurd that they are taxing businesses here and they're going to subsidise things that look like jobs over here. Just stop doing the taxing".
She said the Tories want to halve employer NI costs "because I talk to businesses who say they really want to employ young people but they just can't afford to anymore and the regulation that the Labour Party has put in place has made it harder".
Milburn will say that if the government does go ahead with a gradual reduction in NI over five years, it should start with businesses such as shops, bars and restaurants.
Retail and hospitality together provide 37% of jobs for young people aged between 16 and 24.

title: Black Friday and tax return scams  - don't fall for these
summary: Tens of thousands of scams are reported to HMRC - so it has advice on how to spot a fake request and refund.
body:
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.
That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.
Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.
Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.
If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need tofile a tax returnby the end of January.
Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.
Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether anemail,external,text message,externalorphone call,externalclaiming to be from HMRC is genuine.
"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.
New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.
There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.
To avoid being caught out, HMRC says:
it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one
it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message
it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest
In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered.
Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy.
"When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check.
"No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy."
The bank also advises doing these four things:
Pause and check, rather than being blinded by a countdown timer
Pay safelyusing a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger
Open an official website or app yourselfrather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts
Talk to a friend, family or your bankif you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed
Doing these things now will help you save money at Christmas

title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
summary: The work and pensions secretary said the level of support currently on offer was too vague.
body:
Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits
The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.
Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".
McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.
But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.
It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.
His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.
Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.
Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.
However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.
Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.
He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.
How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.
Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.
Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense'
Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."
He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."
He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".
Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.
Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.
But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".
She added it was "absurd" the government hadincreased taxes for employersin order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.
Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:
a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government
GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work
ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms
It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.
From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.
It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24earlier this year.

title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
summary: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
body:
The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker.
Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers.
The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.
Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements.
"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.
The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.
The reset means they will be dismantled.
In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them".
Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power.
Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer
The prime minister has saidhe believes there is a "win-win" dealto be had with the EU.
Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said the deal would help bring down costs for firms importing food.
"This will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves," he said.
He said currently "pages and pages" of form-filling meant some suppliers had given up exporting to the EU and some products, such as Lincolnshire sausages, meant they were almost impossible to export at all.
Some M&S trucks require over 300 pages of documents for food exports, from export health certificates, phytosanitary certificates, visits from vets and border check paperwork.
Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.
"The amount of paperwork you would need to do, the amount of uncertainty - you have to have it in the right pen colour, if it's not black, it might be refused," Falconer said.
"If you're selling Cox apples from Kent, they have to wait a day before they go into the European Union."
The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.
Falconer said the impact of the reset deal for food would be an additional £5bn.
The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.
This wider agreement includes aligning emissions trading rules, and agreeing to a youth mobility scheme, as well as the reset on food trading.
Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU
Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.
Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.
But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.
He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.
UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.
Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.
Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.
He said there were bound to be compromises and trade-offs in any deal but that where the UK had advantages the government wanted to make sure "those aren't lost under the deal".
Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.
"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.
Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.
Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.
"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.
"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

title: Cut national insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
summary: The report being launched this week will suggest gradually reducing employment costs over five years.
body:
Alan Milburn's report will also make recommendations on cutting the benefits bill
National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say.
A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality.
Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise.
But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".
The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill.
Milburn has said the government spends £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.
He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales.
Milburn wants the government to providea legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support. Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits.
Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them.
The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.
But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow".
Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.
Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.
But Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns three salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and the minimum wage.
She said she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any. Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff.
Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".
Salon-owner Collette Osborne says she is "inundated" with CVs from young people
She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.
"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.
Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.
"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."
Milburn told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme he agreed with a recent move by Chancellor John Healey to slow down the equalisation of the national minimum wage across age groups.
Labour had pledged in its manifesto to remove "discriminatory age bands" and close the gap between adult minimum wages and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.
But in his Budget, Healey said pay for that age group would rise from £10.85 to £11.27 an hour in April next year while people aged 21 and over will see their wages increase from £12.71 to £13.21.
"I understand why because nobody wants to see young workers on poverty pay," Milburn said, but he said it "imposed a lot of costs on [the] government".
"I think we have got to look very carefully at the convergence issue," he said.
Milburn said he supported the government subsidising wages to encourage businesses to take on young workers.
"Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, if you're a small business that's a cost that you've got to absorb," he said.
"The state has a responsibility to help them with that."
On Sunday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government would extend its subsidised jobs guarantee scheme for 18 to 24-year-olds who are claiming Universal Credit.
People who have been on benefits for 12 months will be eligible, down from 18 months and the scheme would be available for people in England, Scotland and Wales.
McFadden said the scheme, which guarantees workers a six-month job, "will help more than 90,000 young people into work by March 2029".
But Whately said it is "just absurd that they are taxing businesses here and they're going to subsidise things that look like jobs over here. Just stop doing the taxing".
She said the Tories want to halve employer NI costs "because I talk to businesses who say they really want to employ young people but they just can't afford to anymore and the regulation that the Labour Party has put in place has made it harder".
Milburn will say that if the government does go ahead with a gradual reduction in NI over five years, it should start with businesses such as shops, bars and restaurants.
Retail and hospitality together provide 37% of jobs for young people aged between 16 and 24.

title: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
summary: The party says its proposals for England aim to address excessive screen time and over-reliance on AI.
body:
The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.
The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that  excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".
The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.
The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofquallaunched a consultation last year,externalon the introduction of on-screen exams.
But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".
In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.
The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".
Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.
Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England
Ministers to issue guidance on children's screen use
The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicianswarned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health".
An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".
Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."
Figures from themost recent government survey,externalshow that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.
The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.
Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."
As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.
A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.
"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.
They added: "Building on the guidance we have published for children under 5, in the new year the department will publish clear guidance on screen use for all children aged 5 to 18, giving parents the advice they need."
A ban on smartphones in schools in England came into force in June, making individual schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.
Education is a devolved matter in the UK, with each of the four nations managing their own systems.
The UK social media ban for under-16s - banning children from major platforms such as  TikTok and Instagram - will come into force in March.

title: UK ethics watchdog chief steps back from role over sexual misconduct claims
summary: The government says Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role after claims made during the early 2000s emerged.
body:
Stuart Sterling was appointed chief executive of the Ethics and Integrity Commission last year
The head of the government's main ethics watchdog has stepped back after it emerged he was investigated in a previous job over alleged sexual misconduct involving female colleagues, and had, in one case, been sanctioned.
Stuart Sterling was appointed as the first chief executive of the newly formed Ethics and Integrity Commission in October 2025.
The existence of the allegations against Sterling, and the investigations into them, were first reported by the Sunday Times.
Following the report, a government spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role while we swiftly establish the facts."
The Labour Party promised in its 2024 manifesto to create the commission to "ensure probity in government" in response to scandals during the Covid pandemic.
As its head, Sterling's role included advising the prime minister on tackling misconduct in public life.
The Sunday Times reported that, in 2003, Sterling had been subject to a "full misconduct hearing" when he was a junior officer with Northamptonshire Police in what was treated as a case "of sexual harassment".
The paper said he had been accused of inappropriately touching the breasts of a female colleague in a police station, and a male colleague who allegedly witnessed the event had reported him to his superiors. It reported that he had been suspended on full pay.
A representative for Mr Sterling said: "Stuart states that a full disciplinary process was held regarding the complaint in 2002. He complied with this fully. It resulted in a sanction."
The Sunday Times reported that he was given a financial penalty of two weeks' pay. It said that, at the time, that was the maximum sanction possible short of forced resignation. He then received two police commendations and was promoted to be a detective sergeant.
The Sunday Times said that by 2008 Mr Sterling had been reported to the force again after another allegation of sexual misconduct against a female colleague, this time at a social gathering outside work.
Mr Sterling's representative said: "He denies that the alleged incident in 2008 ever took place. He was never subject to any criminal investigation, but the allegation was examined by professional standards".
The representative added: "He was not required to resign from the force. He left voluntarily".
Northamptonshire Police has confirmed that it holds a digital record of a misconduct process from 2002.
It did not comment on the later allegation.
In 2009, Sterling joined the Cabinet Office. It is not clear what vetting process he underwent. He has since served in a variety of senior roles and in 2019 was seconded to the National Police Chiefs' Council. In 2023 he received an OBE for helping to plan the funeral of Queen Elizabeth.
It is understood the Cabinet Office will now examine whether appropriate and correct disclosures of information were made.
